title: Why Are Cargo Ships Red Below the Waterline?
description:
Look at almost any big cargo ship in port, and you will see the same thing. Black or blue on top, and a band of red below, right down to the keel. Container ships, tankers, bulk carriers, all red underneath. It is not a fashion. That red is a weapon, in a war against tiny animals that has lasted for centuries. Today, ten parts of a cargo ship's hull, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:04 1. The red paint
2:14 2. The copper sheathing
3:17 3. The banned paint
4:25 4. The barnacles
5:29 5. The boot top
6:30 6. The draft marks
7:33 7. The slippery coating
8:39 8. The dry dock
9:44 9. The ballast water system
10:51 10. The twistlocks
11:57 The verdict

Sources:
- Antifouling paint, copper oxide, self-polishing coatings, foul-release coatings: Wikipedia, "Anti-fouling paint" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-fouling_paint
- Copper sheathing, shipworm, Royal Navy 1760s: Wikipedia, "Copper sheathing" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_sheathing and "Shipworm" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipworm
- TBT, Arcachon oysters, IMO AFS Convention (2008): Wikipedia, "Tributyltin" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tributyltin and IMO https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Environment/Pages/Anti-fouling.aspx
- Biofouling and fuel consumption: Wikipedia, "Biofouling" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biofouling
- Boot topping: Wikipedia, "Boot topping" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boot_topping
- Draft marks and draft surveys: Wikipedia, "Draft (hull)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draft_(hull) and "Draft survey" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draft_survey
- Dry docks: Wikipedia, "Dry dock" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dry_dock
- Ballast Water Management Convention (in force 2017), zebra mussels: Wikipedia, "Ballast water discharge and the environment" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballast_water_discharge_and_the_environment
- Twistlocks and container lashing: Wikipedia, "Twistlock" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twistlock
